subsubtopic: SATELLITE TELEVISION SIGNALS-EQUAL PRIVILEGES THROUGHOUT CANADA-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of recent statements by the chairman of the CRTC, confirmed by the Minister of Communications, that the government will prosecute certain organizations and individuals for distributing television signals received from satellites, but that other groups need not be concerned about prosecution, and since this obvious double standard allows some Canadians the right to choose freely what they watch on television while denying that freedom to others, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):
That the government be directed to prepare amendments to the Canadian Broadcasting Act which recognize the global realities of modern communications technology and which will eliminate the present double standard by extending equal rights and privileges to television viewers in all parts of Canada.

That this House urge the government to place agriculture at the top of the high priorities' list.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the Minister of Transport a question in his responsibility for the Canadian Wheat Board.
I am sure the minister is aware of the severe drop in price received by farmers since the embargo placed on shipments to the U.S.S.R. by the previous government, and continued by this government, because of the unconscionable attack by the U.S.S.R. on Afghanistan. Can the minister explain to me, other members of this House and the farmers of western Canada the plans he has to compensate them for this loss of income?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am quite aware of the fact that following the U.S.S.R. aggression in Afghanistan, the Canadian government at the time took action to restrain Canadian exports. With respect to the degree of compensation that this might justify, which is an acceptable principle inasmuch as reduction in export and price can be directly related to the restraint of export to the Soviet Union, this is constantly being assessed by the government.
It is too early now, because there is still a month and a half to go before the end of the season, to find out exactly what the effect of the government's action has been. However, as I said, this is constantly being monitored. There will be a cabinet paper in a few weeks, at the end of the grain season.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: In light of the minister's acceptance of the principle of compensating farmers in western Canada, and in light of his policy and the policy of the previous government to monitor continually the change in price, I am sure the minister realizes that since January the farmers of western Canada have suffered a reduction of approximately 75 cents per bushel for their grain. Can the minister tell me how many reports he, his assistant in the other place, or the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce have received to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: On what, may I ask?

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I would like to draw to the attention of the minister a statement made on January 9 by his assistant in the other place, who said that farmers must be compensated for their loss of income and a monitoring policy must be set up to arrive at that figure.
Can the minister tell me, the members of this House and the farmers of western Canada whether anyone has monitored this situation? Has his department, or the Department of Agriculture, monitored it? If they have not monitored it, why have they not answered questions put to them, in light of the 75-cent reduction per bushel of grain for farmers of western Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the monitoring system is obviously a collective action. This is done through the grains group, which is a unit that belongs to Agriculture, Transport, and Industry, Trade and Commerce. It is being done there. Before coming to a conclusion, obviously all the facts must be put together. As I said a moment ago, it is too early now, because sales may be made to countries other than the U.S.S.R. in the coming month and a half, to come to that conclusion.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the same minister on the same topic. The fact is that prices have dropped approximately 75 cents a bushel since January 4, when the embargo was put in place. That is a fact; it does not need to be monitored.
In these circumstances, why was the Canadian Wheat Board not represented at a meeting in Brussels on May 19 to discuss the subject, among many others, of the embargo which was placed on shipments of grain following the invasion of Afghanistan? Seventy-five cents a bushel has been lost. Is this not a sufficient basis upon which the government could go ahead with a policy of ensuring that the farmers of western Canada do not carry the full price-tag for Canada's foreign policy?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: This decision was made by the previous government and it is supported by the present government; there is no doubt about that. Obviously, the previous government knew that the decision made last January would have certain effects on volumes and on prices. That is why they put forward the idea of compensation.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: What about Brussels?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext: Thank you very much. I will deal with these points one after another. I thank the Leader of the Opposition for his advice. On this subject, there was a meeting of exporters in Brussels in May and the Canadian government was represented there by the head of the Grains Group, which is not abnormal in these instances.

subsubtopic: COMPENSATION FOR FARMERS DUE TO EMBARGO ON SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.
speechtext:
I am concerned because the Canadian Wheat Board should have been at that meeting in Brussels, not necessarily a government official. Perhaps I should turn to the Minister of Agriculture, since the responses we have had from the Minister of Transport in relation to his responsibilities in this House on behalf of the Canadian Wheat Board have been totally inadequate.
In the light of a Statistics Canada report today showing that farm income fell drastically in the month of April, can the hon. gentleman take it upon himself to see that this 75 cents a bushel which has been lost by western grain producers will be forthcoming to them, in line with the policy now adhered to as a result of the statement by the Minister of Transport?

EMBARGO ON GRAIN SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.-INTENTIONS FOR NEXT CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my supplementary is to the Minister of Transport who answers for the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. There is one other dimension to this whole question that has not yet been raised today; that is, the whole question of whether Canada is prepared to continue the embargo that we entered into at the first of the year.
The minister may know there is concern at the present time by farm groups in western Canada that maybe they have not been treated as fairly as they could have been. With excess capacity developing in the transportation system, if we do continue the embargo into the next crop year we could, in effect, find ourselves out of sales we might have been able to make if we had not followed this line. Has the government given any consideration to what it intends to do after the end of this crop year?

speakerposition: Minister of Transport
subtopic: EMBARGO ON GRAIN SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.-INTENTIONS FOR NEXT CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Very much, Madam Speaker, because obviously we have to decide now if we are going to continue the restraint action in the next crop year. Nobody likes the restraint situation we are in now; everybody would love to sell a lot more. But the decision of January last was made because of political circumstances; that is, the invasion of Afghanistan.
Obviously, the great eagerness of everybody related to this industry to export more and more, to the Soviet Union in particular, must be assessed in the light of political events that took place originally to justify the restraint period. That is going on now in the cabinet, and before the end of the crop year, presumably, a decision will be made as to whether the restraint period should continue.

subtopic: EMBARGO ON GRAIN SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.-INTENTIONS FOR NEXT CROP YEAR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, is the minister saying to the House that the government, through the cabinet, is not prepared to, or will not make any changes in policy when the new crop year arrives after July 31? Is the decision to continue well into 1980, and possibly 1981?

subtopic: EMBARGO ON GRAIN SHIPMENTS TO U.S.S.R.-INTENTIONS FOR NEXT CROP YEAR
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my understanding is that the restraint period was for the duration of this crop year. As we will be confronted with a new crop year on August 1, presumably a decision will have to be made on whether the restraint period should continue into the new crop year: it is elementary.

speakeroldname: Mr. D. M. Collenette (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subsubtopic: CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES
speechtext:
The conflict of interest guidelines for ministers, in effect since April 28, 1980, require that:
IV Gifts
"Ministers shall disclose in the public registry any personal gift or other benefit of a value exceeding $200 which they receive from any person not connected with them by blood relationship, marriage or adoption, together with the name and address of the donor. Official gifts and hospitality received from other governments and hospitality received from personal friends are not subject to this rule. All gifts or benefits exceeding $200 in value, other than official gifts or benefits, are to be declared to the ADRG within 30 days of their receipt for disclosure in the public registry."
The guidelines for ministers also require that:
V1U Administration
"-Ministers must complete all arrangements necessary to achieve full compliance within 120 days of appointment or of the coming into force of these guidelines. Within this time period, ministers must provide to the ADRG copies of duly executed trust instruments and public disclosures of previous activities, personal gifts or benefits and disclose-able assets, as required, and a public document in which they will indicate in summary for the arrangements they have made to comply with these guidelines. The public disclosures of previous activities, personal gifts or benefits and disclose-able assets and the summary of arrangements made by a minister will be open to examination by the general public in the public registry maintained by the ADRG."
Information about the disclosure of gifts and benefits by ministers may be sought from the public registry maintained by the assitant deputy registrar general at the Trafalgar Building, 4th Floor, 207 Queen Street, Ottawa, soon after the expiry of the 120 day compliance period referred to above.

speechtext:
The House resumed, from Monday, June 9, consideration in committee of Bill C-19, to amend the Employment Tax Credit Act-Mr. Axworthy-Mr. Blaker in the chair.
On clause 1-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: When the committee rose on Monday, June 9, 1980, clause 1 of the bill was under consideration. I believe the hon. member for Calgary West had the floor.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is our third day of Committee of the Whole examination of this bill. I want once again to remind the House that I see no officials present. I also want again to remind the House that we have requested that the minister either be better briefed or show up in this committee with officials. It is our contention that the minister wastes the time of the committee because he does not have the answers to the reasonable questions which we on this side and those on his side are putting to him.
I wish to quote from Hansard for December 4, 1979, page 1995:
Our objection to this bill rests both on the substance of it and on the attitude of the government. They have not shown during the debate on this bill any co-operation and openness-
The quote is from the minister when he was sitting in opposition and debating our mortgage tax credit bill. I think it summarizes a great deal of the feeling that is building up on this side of the chamber. We have to look at that feeling in the context of the present situation.
Back in 1972-73, I remind the minister, the Liberal government was facing an unemployment situation of a little more than half a million people. In that context, in a public policy sense, for one program alone, the local initiatives program, a job creation program, they were willing to allocate 1 per cent of the budget funds available to the government. Here we are, eight years later with the worst unemployment situation that this country has ever faced, with a rapidly worsening employment situation, and we find the government proposing some ten days ago in this House an expenditure for job creation that is less than one quarter of 1 per cent of federal government expenditures.
June 11, 1980

It is in that context that it is not only the right of members of Parliament to be able to examine with the minister his proposed legislation, but it is clearly an obligation. When his government chooses to allocate to job creation so few funds, such a little amount of money, it is the obligation of those on this side to examine very carefully whether that money will be well spent.
It is in that context that I rise today and begin another series of questions. I wish to begin with the minister's statement this morning made to a women's group in this city. 1 quote from a press release:
They were restricted-
That refers to his government.
-to spending limits-
That is in the context of job creation.
-set by the former Progressive Conservative government and he is not willing to announce an expensive new deal until a full review of existing programs is complete some time next fall.
I begin by asking the minister how he comes to the conclusion that the decision that he and his cabinet makes as what to spend on job creation is a consequence of the spending limits established by the Conservative government. Can he tell us how he comes to that conclusion?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the answer to that question is quite obvious, that the estimates of spending were established by the previous government. We were working within those spending estimates. What we did was shift the priority within those estimates to apply a different program, allocating them in terms of direct job creation as opposed to the employment tax credit.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I sat in this House in early April. I heard the Minister of Finance increase the federal budget to the tune of $2 billion. Can the minister tell us what portion of that $2 billion increase he got for job creation?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the hon. member is repeating the question he raised in question period yesterday. I pointed out to him in question period in repetition, which seems to be the only way to get the answer through, that in fact the increased expenditures were allocated to a number of job stimulation measures. He seems to be under the illusion that the only form of job creation was that announced last Monday. It has been repeated to him time and time again that in fact there is a wide variety of economic stimulation measures taking place in the government, that we believe in a mixed approach to job creation, particularly in terms of investing in long-term job creation. If the hon. member is prepared to look at the variety of decisions taken over the past three months, he will see exactly where those expenditures have been made.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 think Hansard records-and the papers given to us by the Minister of Finance say the same thing-that the increased $2 billion expenditure was to go to the subsidy paid for the consumption of oil and to pay interest on the public debt. Is the minister disagreeing with that
Employment Tax Credit Act
statement by the Minister of Finance? Is he suggesting to the committee that from that $2 billion extra expenditure he got some of the money for his operations?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Perhaps I might repeat what I said, Mr. Chairman. The budget account adds up to well over $60 billion. Within that sum a wide variety of initiatives are taken by the government to assist in economic stimulation and job investment from one end of the country to the other. The global budget is attached to a vast variety of purposes, as he will see if the hon. member would like to go through the estimates. I invite him to attend a variety of meetings which are held daily to examine the spending estimates of a number of departments. I am sure it would be a very useful exercise for him to attend those committee meetings and add up the large number of jobs which have been created as a consequence of government expenditure.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Is the minister suggesting that paying a subsidy on oil imports or paying increased interest on the public debt creates jobs in this country? Is that the kind of economics he is giving us this afternoon?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not use the same kind of silly logic as does the hon. member. I am saying that within the budget of the Government of Canada a number of initiatives are taken to create jobs. If the hon. member wants to quarrel with the principle of providing one-price oil across Canada rather than require the maritimes to pay substantially higher prices, I suggest he should take that issue up with the caucus before he speaks publicly on it.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am very much concerned about the employment situation in the Atlantic region. One of the criticisms of this bill is that it does so little for areas of high unemployment in this country. I was in the House earlier during the question period today and heard the minister of energy propose that oil should be available at one price to all Canadians. On the surface that sounds very good, but it has an impact on job creation. Two provinces in this confederation, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island, depend on electricity for much of the energy which their industries use. In those two provinces electricity is generated by oil. The consequence of one-price oil in Canada is that people in those two provinces will pay twice as much for electricity, whether they use it in their homes or in their businesses. A one-price policy would, in effect, make it much more difficult for Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island to attract industry. Is the minister saying he is prepared to go to the minister of energy and argue for a special subsidy for the generation of electrical power in those two provinces?

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
The hon. member somehow has the habit of making an assertion, drawing a conclusion and then putting the words in my mouth. If he finds this an amusing exercise, I have no objection. But what he says ought not to be taken seriously as being in any way a statement of our policy. I simply respond that the reason there is one price is to make

June 11, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
sure there is some degree of unity across this country, that some degree of parity between the regions is maintained. The cost of doing so is what we pay for maintaining a degree of equality in Canada, and if the hon. member is not prepared to pay it he should have a serious discussion with his leader and his caucus, because he is certainly way out in right field.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
It is nice to be in the field instead of out of the field, Mr. Chairman. The principle of equality is an important one and the minister is demonstrating either a lack of capacity to listen or an unwillingness to respond. If we are to disperse jobs in this country, if there is to be equality of opportunity in the different regions, one of the most important parts of that industrial dispersion is the supply of energy and its price.
It was a Liberal government some 15 years ago, I believe, which provided incentives for Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island to switch from coal-fired electrical generation to oil-fired generation because it was cheaper to import oil than to use the domestic supply. The situation today is that imported oil costs more than double the cost of domestic, and the areas to which I have referred burn this oil for the purpose of generating electricity. When a one-price policy for oil is in effect, it will be the same for all Canadians who want to buy gasoline for their cars but it will not be the same for all Canadians in terms of heating their homes or running factories in Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island. In those provinces the price will be doubled. This will affect the ability of a region to attract employers.
Mr. Chairman, I want to move on now to the five basic issues we should keep foremost in mind when looking at employment programs of any kind. First, there is the question of timing. Will the measure which is introduced spend the money and create jobs at the right time? Second, is this the best way to spend money? Will it provide the most employment and the best kind of employment for the least dollar cost? Third, we should ask ourselves: What is the value of the goods or services provided by this additional employment? Fourth, is the money being spent to provide employment for people who really need it as opposed to those who may not need it so much? Finally, what will the impact of this increased employment, this increased spending, be on inflation?
I should like to go back to the first of those questions. I should like to go back to the first question I asked in this chamber on the last occasion when the predecessor bill was before a committee and to the same question I asked the first time this bill was before a committee. I am interested in knowing what planning figures the minister is using to predict when we are likely to peak. In what month and in what year are we likely to experience the highest number of unemployed Canadians? Will it be 1981, 1980, 1982, 1983? Which month of which year is the minister using as the date on which we are likely to experience the highest unemployment? This occurs in the context of the timing-whether or not this bill asks Parliament to endorse the spending of money when it is needed most. The minister has the figures; he refused to share them
with us on a previous occasion. 1 hope he may be more forthcoming today.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Chairman, I am glad the hon. member finally got around to reading my opening address because the principles he put forward were those contained in my opening statement. So it is nice to know that after 20 hours of debate he has finally got around to understanding what the purpose of the employment tax credit bill is.
He still avoids one basic point, however, which is this. The employment tax credit bill does not represent the entire package we are putting forward as employment measures. It is one of several initiatives we have put forward and I would again remind the hon. member that this is simply an extension of the existing tax credit program until we have had the time and the opportunity to examine properly the changes which are taking place in the economy of this country and have reviewed federal programs through a variety of procedures.
We are extending this legislation for the following reason. When this government came to office there were no job creation programs in existence. Canada Works was cancelled and phased out, and the hon. member who has been belabouring his acute concern about the plight of the Atlantic provinces is a member of the same government which cancelled the Canada Works program, which would have created jobs directly and have been of major benefit in the Atlantic provinces and in the eastern portion of Quebec.
He cannot have it both ways. He cannot come here and flail away at the inadequacy of our programs when he belonged to a government which cancelled the very programs which were a major benefit to that region. He was a member of a caucus then. Did he stand up in caucus and complain about what an awful thing my predecessor was doing in cancelling those programs? I did not hear him say anything in Parliament about that. I did not see him rise to his feet in righteous indignation concerning the awful measures which were being taken to void completely an area of its major employment programs. I suggest that he has gone through a little Saul of Tarsus routine. He has changed his mind, as people are apt to do when they change sides in the House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: It happened to you, Lloyd.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Perhaps the hon. member is learning from a good teacher. The fact of the matter is, Mr. Chairman, and we repeat it again, that we have put into place in this country not just the employment tax credit program, which is designed to provide job availabilities for close to 50,000 participants in the next year. We have also put into effect a number of direct job-creation measures which go on top of those already in existence. We are spending well over $116 billion in this department on a variety of training and job measures.
Now, if the hon. member thinks that is inadequate, he should be debating that entire package and not picking out one piece or another. I would suggest, Mr. Chairman, that this is
June 11, 1980

not the place to do that, just as it is not the place to debate energy policy or all the other irrelevancies that have been brought into this debate in the last 24 hours of the time of the House. This bill has consumed that much time primarily because the hon. member opposite is asking the same questions over and over and getting the exact answers he wants but not registering them on whatever litmus paper he uses to record these things.
The fact of the matter is that when it comes to the assessment of what we are expecting in the unemployment field, the statistics are in front of hon. members opposite. I do not have to keep providing them to them. They get them every month from Statistics Canada. The patterns are there. We know that the seasonal variations of employment rise and fall according to conditions of seasonal employment in winter, summer, spring and fall. Furthermore, Mr. Chairman, we are very vulnerable and sensitive to the decisions made outside our boundaries. We cannot in any way control the decisions of the U.S. federal reserve board that were made last year to hike interest rates up to 20 per cent, causing a recession in the United States, which caused a downturn in their economy, causing them to buy less pulp and paper, less lumber and less manufactured goods, thus creating an unemployment problem in Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, we do not have control over the United States. We could influence them-my hon. colleague who just left, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce, does his best-but we are not in any way going to try to pretend that we are omnipotent when it comes to economic matters, just as the hon. member's government was not omnipotent. No government is omnipotent.
All I am saying is that the hon. member for Calgary West is asking questions that have been answered fully both by the Minister of Finance in his initial statement and by myself in repeating those statements. We told him what we expect the unemployment rate in this country to be. It will be at the level of about 8 per cent. He said that he does not agree and that it will be 9 per cent. That is up to him. Wood Gundy has its figures. The reason economics is a dismal science is because everyone has a gloomy prediction to make, and they are all different. However, that is our best forecast for next year. Mr. Chairman, 1 will not predict beyond that. 1 am not going to vault myself into crystal balling into 1983, 1984 or 1985.
Part of the reason, in case it has escaped the notice of the hon. member, that we are doing the review is to come up with those very assessments so that we can establish proper calculations and reorient our programs accordingly. That is why we are doing it. He is a member of a parliamentary committee to do that kind of study. I think, Mr. Chairman, he should curb his impatience, proceed in a logical, rational manner to get representations from across this country and join with his parliamentary colleagues and present the proper report, which 1 would be very glad to receive.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have reviewed Hansard for the last two committee meetings, and I find a perfect correla-
Employment Tax Credit Act
tion and a perfect relationship between the lack of knowledge on the minister's part and the length of his answers.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext: Order, please. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, on my point of order, I asked a question, and I think an examination of Hansard will indicate that the minister took some considerable time and did not answer my question.
Is it part of my 20 minutes when he chooses not to answer my question or do I still get a chance to ask additional questions? Can he eat up all my time by talking about something different from what I asked?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Order, please. It is well understood that the Chair does not comment upon the quality or lack thereof of either the questions or the answers in the House of Commons, except in some reference to parliamentary language and matters of that nature.
Certainly some hon. members who are questioning might far prefer to have the majority of their time dedicated to questions, with the smallest possible amount of time dedicated to answers. Other hon. members might feel the opposite way. The time allotted is 20 minutes, and the manner in which it is used is the business of the hon. member and the minister, not that of the Chair.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my question is to the hon. minister. I do not wish to belabour this point, but I think that something has to be cleared up from when questions stopped the last day.
This is a very simple act. All it is is an employment tax credit program. What I am trying to point out is that I feel that $100 million in the total program is being targeted to areas, as the minister has indicated himself. We do not know what is happening with this tax credit program, but it is still a loss of revenue to the government of $100 million. Perhaps 60 per cent, according to the minister's best estimates, are using it. Can we afford to carry this program and gamble $40 million or just throw it away? That is what we are doing, and that is the point I am making.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member brings up a good question. The only thing I would ask is that he try to straighten it out with his colleague from Calgary West, who suggested in the House that a direct job creation program is a waste of money and that a tax credit program is a more efficient use of our money. However, that is something between the two of them. I must confess that I have some of the same reservations about the use of the tax credit methodology. It is one that is widely used in a number of countries, and the evaluations have shown that the actual incremental number of

June 11, 1980
Employment Tax Credit Act
jobs can range between 20 per cent and 50 per cent in those areas. We have estimated, in interim reports that we have had, that it was around 60 per cent. As I indicated, a full evaluation will be done upon the completion of the cycle of this program, if the bill passes, which we hope to have by the end of the summer. I did indicate to the hon. member that I would provide that report to him. Sixty per cent is a judgment call in part based upon the auditing that we do through the Department of National Revenue. But we do ask for the base line employees and the actual numbers.
All I can indicate to the hon. member is that again, as I said, we do not have the ability to pry into the minds of some 18,000 businessmen who have signed up agreements under this program as to whether they were going to hire people in any event. They have to sign certificates saying it is incremental work, and I would suspect from the monitoring that we have done that there is a fair amount of it. That is the reason, Mr. Chairman, why we did not want to put all our eggs into the one basket of the employment tax credit.
That is why we wanted to vary the program and test it out. It is certainly my intention, again through the review process we are initiating, to get calculations from other areas and try to develop a more in-the-field observation from our own regional offices as to the actual incremental number of jobs put into the work force as a consequence of the tax credit.
I might say that there might be a particular value not just in the general employment field, but again in trying to target in on special needs. There are groups of people in the labour force who we know are more difficult to employ either because of lack of skills or because of certain work handicaps they may suffer, and tax credits may be a way of providing a direct incentive to the employer to bring those people into the work force. That will be one of the areas of examination we will be making in this review in terms of prescribing longer term programs.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in the minister's words, I made some serious charges when I said that 1 felt the program was being abused. I want to really clear up this situation. I am not casting aspersions on the businessmen who sign up for the program, nor am I casting aspersions on the department itself. What I am suggesting is that someone from the manpower offices who is responsible for the program may be overzealous and go out and solicit. We mentioned before that in a high growth area the employer would never even think of applying for this program if he did not get someone from the manpower office knocking on his door and saying, "This is a new job and you qualify for this program." The businessman is not at fault here. I am saying that somehow something breaks down, and 1 think that is where the abuse comes in.
I have done some more checking myself. The minister said that he has checked in offices in my riding. I would like to know how he checked the people who were going out and asking employers to take part in the program because it was a high growth area.
I should like to suggest also to the hon. member for South West Nova, who mentioned that there were not many employers there taking part in the program, that they do not do so because these are high growth areas. That is what I think is wrong with the tax credit program. The only guys who are going to use it are those who are making the bucks. It is of no use to someone who is breaking even.

speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Minister of Employment and Immigration
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would say to the hon. member for Athabasca that his observation may be a proper one. We have several thousand employers and you cannot monitor them every day if someone is being overzealous in promoting the program and suggesting its benefits could be used, not in the way the program is designed, but in a way simply to add an additional employee to the factory, we would want to correct that abuse.
We did check with the employment offices in the hon. member's riding to determine that, and we were not able to get any evidence. I would simply suggest to him again that we unquestionably did undertake a major promotion of the program, because when it was first introduced in 1978 there was not much uptake. I think the program produced only 16,000 places. Since then we have been able to increase it to around 50,000. I am sure that within that number there are some who may be abusing it.
If the hon. member has suggestions as to how we can ensure that the abuses are not extended, without increasing the red tape or the regulations, I would be very glad to hear them. I hope it is something on which we will be able to get a better fix as we look at the program more carefully over the summer and fall months. Perhaps this is something for which the parliamentary committee in its hearings across the country may get a better idea.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
I am glad the minister pointed out that the number went up from 16,000 to 45,000. That is my whole point. I think the 16,000 probably was a realistic level where the program was unsolicited from the employer. I am wondering if it was advertised, whether people were informed by way of brochures, rather than have someone go out as a salesman to the employer's office saying, "This program is available, you are expanding, new jobs are being created and you fall under this program."
I am not suggesting for a moment that the individual who goes out from the manpower office is attempting to do something illegal. I am not suggesting that the employer feels he is doing something illegal. He feels that he falls under this program because it is brought out to him and explained in this way, and this is an education program, as the minister mentioned. I should like to suggest that no one go out from the manpower office, that it should be advertised in the paper and that brochures be sent out. That is my point.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING EXTENSION OF PROGRAM PERIOD
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have a few brief questions because in the previous Parliament it was my privilege to have had the responsibility of being the minister of employment and immigration when this program was initiated. When the pro-
June 11, 1980

gram was initiated, we built in a lot of road blocks and there was too much red tape. As a result of that, the program was not working, so we called in the business community and asked them what was wrong with it. They said there was too much red tape, there were too many road blocks. We were being pressured constantly by a very good critic, namely, the former member for Hamilton West, who indicated that we should remove some of this red tape. This was asked by the opposition parties who said, "For heaven sake, trust the businessmen. These people out there are not crooks. They want to work, they want to create the jobs, but they will not go through all this red tape in the interest of proving their honesty." So we followed that particular program.
In the first instance, I think the program was taken up in large measure in the province of Quebec. We checked with our people there to find out why it was being taken up in Quebec and found that the reason was the leadership given by some officials in the Department of Employment and Immigration who let the businessmen know that this plan was available to them, that they could hire people, that there was a tax credit available to them. Then we removed much of the red tape, not only at the behest of the opposition parties but at the behest of the Canadian business community. As a result of that, the program took off and became very successful.
We did not have all of the protection built in that we had in the original instance, but we felt that the Canadian businessman could be trusted. I think that the figures we are hearing today from the minister are accurate to the degree that they can be. I believe it was last Friday that the hon. member for Bow River made what I think were the only remarks on the subject of farm labour in these proceedings in Committee of the Whole. The minister may remember them. I think they were appropriate remarks. He spoke from experience and long years of a genuine interest in the subject. At that time he reminded the committee about the problem of perhaps inexperienced and new farm helpers which are available from time to time through employment offices for work on farms. Also he mentioned the concern of the farmer employer about very, very expensive modern-day equipment. He spoke of tractors and implements that were worth up to $30,000.
I share that concern, but I want to comment a little more about the type of manpower I can hopefully get from manpower offices which might be of more help to us in the cattle business. It is not an easy job to convince young people, especially, to come out into the country and work on a cattle ranch. This is not a critical comment about the minister and his department, but there are valid reasons for this situation,

Of course, the reasons for this relate to the fact that those kinds of jobs are a long way from the bright lights, especially for young people. I can tell members that that is a major factor in this day and age. Another reason is that it comes as quite a shock to a young person, whose idea of cattle ranching is an image he has picked up from watching western movies on television, that we have to work in the winter and keep ourselves warm outdoors all day. He loses his enthusiasm in a hurry when that situation becomes apparent to him.
We in the cattle business have the same problem with respect to expensive machinery. We hesitate to allow inexperienced help to operate that machinery, even if we are resigned to that fact. I am thinking of a modern-day, 14-foot, self-propelled hay swather which can be worth up to $35,000. We are faced with the same situation. It is just as significant that we have trained stock horses. Sometimes it takes five, six or seven years to properly train a stock horse to work with cattle. We hesitate about allowing inexperienced help to ride and use those horses.
The type of labour in which I am interested for my own operation is full-time, year-round help. When we hire them, we hope it is by the year and that they stay for ten years. Of course, experienced help who would qualify in these areas are very difficult to hire. If they are very experienced they work on their own, which is understandable. A few times I have gone to the manpower office and have been successful in getting help. More recently I find the local officials seem to feel that they should specify a minimum wage which as a prospective employer I should be expected to pay. A good question is: How much is an experienced man worth?
My own experience in this specialized field is that I always have to pay more than perhaps the going rate in order to entice them, if you like, to come out and work on a cattle ranch. But it becomes a little annoying when Manpower officials suggest that there is a certain wage, regardless of whether one agrees with it or not, that is expected to be maintained. I should like to ask the minister whether that is official policy and what comments he might have on that.

I will make a point in those negotiations to raise some of the concerns about agricultural training.
I should like to make one comment to the hon. member which perhaps is something that goes back to his view of the attitude of young Canadian people toward working on farms. We operate an exchange program of farm students between certain European countries and our own. Several weeks ago I met with the sponsors of that program. They indicated that they can recruit enough trained and interested students from Europe, but that they cannot attract similar numbers of Canadian students to go overseas to learn about farm methods in Denmark, The Netherlands, the Scandinavian countries or West Germany. They feel that one of the reasons is that there seems to be a negative attitude toward going into farm work at the present time. It is something we will have to address and perhaps something our department, in combination with the Minister of Agriculture, can look at.

Mr. Chairman, the problem with the LIP, LEAP and OFY type of grants is that they are generally of short duration. It can even be claimed that they sometimes create havoc in the lives of participants through a sense of insecurity. People do not have the opportunity to buy a home
and establish a permanent lifestyle because they never know whether the grants will be renewed or what sort of changes may be made in the programs and the philosophies of the government. It is often found that people who exist on grants acquire a great expertise in "grantmanship" and that a lot of their abilities are wasted.
It is not a very wise thing to use community groups to provide needed social and human services, particularly as they relate to native communities. It is better if they are trained to do these things themselves and they are often in the best position to help themselves. It is only good sense to encourage this approach.
The major problem with all these programs is that they are short term and it is not known whether they will continue from one year to the next. Often they are programs that deliver essential social services that the government cannot provide. All too often the services of social welfare departments and hospitals are inaccessible to the native people because of the cultural alienation that exists. It is only sensible to provide human services to the native organizations through the native communities. It appears to me to be cynical to make them short-term projects. This creates disillusionment and a sense that they are receiving gifts for which they must plead and connive, bow and scrape for, rather than giving them the feeling that they are getting money to supply services that they have a right to.
I would ask the minister to give serious consideration to the short-time factor that is involved in the job creation type of program and to ask his department for proposals that would allow long-term funding for native organizations. I wonder if the minister could respond to this suggestion.

Mr. Chairman, I agree with the hon. member that one of the main objectives of members of this House should be to try to break that horrendous cycle of dependency and poverty that native people in this country experience, but it will not take place overnight.
If the hon. member has been following the announcements made by several of my colleagues, he will know that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has indicated that he wants to restore a sense of autonomy and independence to band councils so that they may make their own economic and social decisions.
We are attempting to come to grips with the question of land claims which would put a substantial amount of capital in the hands of native organizations and band councils and give them a major source of money for investment so that they may develop their own programs and resources.
I agree with the direction that the hon. member recommends we take and indeed we are trying to move that way. I would ask him to reflect upon some of the initiatives we have taken recently through my department to begin the process of longer-term economic development. Through the local economic development assistance program we intend to set up a series of projects across Canada designed to help communities establish economic development corporations which will enable
June 11, 1980

them to initiate the analysis and marketing feasibility studies necessary for their communities and to obtain the seed capital to invest in new business opportunities.
It is my hope and ambition that these pilot projects will show how we can expand the whole concept of economic development for native people, as opposed to short-term assistance.
I do not think we should disregard or deny, however, the value of the shorter-term job-creation programs. 1 put this question very explicitly to native leaders when they were in this city three or four weeks ago at the council of chiefs meeting. I asked whether they wanted us to cancel the job-creation programs and the universal answer was that they did not. They considered them necessary for two reasons. First, they provided work as opposed to being on the pogey. In many cases the work is in and around the reserves, which is very valuable. A number of the projects concern the development of roads, transportation systems, sewer systems, public works programs and so on. The hon. member has visited many of the same reserves that I have and he knows that many of them need substantial public works improvements.
More important is the fact that the short-term job-creation programs also provide job experience in new settings for native people. It is often the first opportunity for them. I can think of a number of projects that I helped get established in my own city when I was working at the university, such as the Winnipeg home improvement project. A LIP grant was used to establish a skill training program in which approximately 80 per cent of the participants were native. We kept track of the program and found that 50 or 60 per cent of the participants found full-time employment. It provided them with their first opportunity to gain on-the-job experience. They acquired certain attitudes and habits which were useful in a new environment.
I do not apologize for the short-term job-creation programs, therefore, and I think we must continue to use them. I do agree, however, that we should shift the emphasis to long-term job creation and in particular allow native people and organizations to make the economic decisions for themselves.

It seems to me that it goes without saying that I should support this bill. I am deeply concerned that this piece of legislation should be passed and passed urgently. It seems to me that we are trying to get under way a program that needs to be continued, and if we do not work and act quickly it will fall by the wayside and its momentum will be lost.
We understand also that this is not the only bill that will deal with unemployment. It is only one weapon in an arsenal of attempts to work with and overcome the problems that face those who are unemployed. It seems to me that if we have any compassion for those who are unemployed and if we really cared, we would not find it necessary to have 20 hours of debate, or more, of constant repetition.

We would not find it necessary to talk about something that has already been tested and used, and whose value has already been realized. To understand what has happened in the past, we see also that it is a program to meet the small businessman's needs and help him fulfil his ability to make a contribution to the private sector, to the whole country and to its employment programs as well.
We see the opportunity here of giving the small businessman an opportunity to participate in the economy and also to help the unemployed. It seems to me that it is a method that has been approved as being one of the few methods which the Conservative party has recommended in terms of dealing with unemployment, because it is to stimulate the economy by stimulating business.
In that respect the principle seems to be good and accepted by all sides. However, if we accept that that is one tool, not the only method of approaching unemployment, and if we also realise the fact that there are many other programs which the Minister of Employment and Immigration has announced that this will be part of a wider package of programs, then we can see that there are other parts that we can look forward to if members do not want this program alone.
In the meantime, we have an urgent situation. If people are unemployed and in need of jobs, why does this House persist in debating something we all understand? A lot of people are wondering about this. People who are watching this debate on television and people who sit in the House know why this is Committee of the Whole and why the whole of Parliament is not here right now. They ask what is happening. Nothing is happening. That is why often all the benches are empty. There is a delay, if you will; there is obstruction in being able to bring forward legislation that deals with urgent needs. There has to be some concern of conscience on the part of all of those who have to think about people who are unemployed as to whether we are really dealing with these issues or toying and playing with them for political ends and purposes.
If we really cared, we would get on with the job. We would get on with the job by passing this particular piece of legislation. Using our committee on employment and immigration which exists for that purpose, we could discuss employment packages, or better packages if we have any. This bill is not aimed at dealing with the whole unemployment problem of Canada; we all know that. We know that it is an urgent bill. It is a transitional one, to keep something going while we bring forward other legislation that would deal later with the total unemployment problem of Canada.
We inherited a situation where there were no funds to deal with these problems at the present time. We have to at least perpetuate what is there and keep it going because it is a good program. We should be able to assess its value. No program is perfect. No one program will solve all problems for all regions. The question is whether this Parliament intends in the next little while to help those urgently in need of that help, and to get a bill through to support a principle on which pretty well everyone has agreed.

Incidentally, that is the first time since I have lived there, almost 30 years, that I can remember this company closing down. Anyway, 10,000 additional people will be laid off. That is the equivalent, under a job-creation program such as this, if we take into account the length of time involved, of 200 year-long jobs disappearing just because all these 10,000 people have been laid off for a week. In addition, there will be a marked reduction in the numbers of people who will be making purchases. One must take account of the fear which accompanies these lay-offs. Many of those affected will be reluctant to resume their normal purchasing patterns bearing in mind that the reason given for the lay-offs is a dramatic decline in markets. This is bound to have an effect upon the sale of goods and the flow of services.
With all this in mind, given that the levels of unemployment in Ontario have risen significantly in the past month, given that most of the unemployment is located in the major industrial areas, given that these areas are where most of the young people who are seeking employment live, given that the major unemployment which is occurring almost inevitably results in a decrease in purchasing at the retail level where many of the young people might find work, can the minister outline what measures he might introduce, perhaps supplementary to the bill now before us, which would begin to address themselves to the situation, now crucial, which presently faces us?

A number of areas-for example, the aerospace industry-are not going to be creating unemployment. The real trick is to make sure we find workers who are unemployed in those areas where labour is needed.

Taking that into account and the fact that because those people are unemployed there will be a reduction in purchasing and that that reduction in purchasing inevitably will lead to fewer job opportunities, what then can you use this kind of program for? Where do those people go to find work? I just mentioned that Dominion Foundries will be laying off 10,000 people for seven days. Dominion Foundries has employed people in the past for summer employment. It is very difficult to imagine how they will employ people this year for summer employment. That means that the people who might normally have been employed there will be looking elsewhere, but for the 10,000 people who are unemployed for a week, that is one one fifty-second part of their income for that year that is affected in one way or another, and so they will be reducing their purchasing. As they reduce their purchasing, the jobs that those young people might normally get in department stores and in other summer-type work will not be available. I do not understand how giving money in the way that we are talking about without having developed an over-all strategy will work.
I do not understand where the jobs will come from. I really do not. I am not trying to create a political argument, 1 am being as honest as I can be. I do not know where those jobs are. If the economy is in a decline, as it is, if the major employers are laying off, as they are, and if that has the depressing effect on the economy that we all understand that it has, then the secondary type of job that is being looked for by these people will not be there. I do not understand how a program like this can possibly work in those circumstances. I think that if we were in a period of increasing employment and increasing purchasing and had a more buoyant economy, then we could reasonably expect to see some job opportunities.
Let me suggest that if the government had gone ahead and decided to embark on a major program of house building, that would have created a number of jobs in related industries. We all know, I am sure, that there has been a marked decline in the number of housing starts, although there is still a considerable demand. With that decline we are now down to something like 170,000 starts projected for this year. That is down from what is generally accepted as being a target of 260,000 that would be required if we were to keep pace with the need.
If the government were to embark on that kind of program and were then to use some of this money to support employment in related industries, I could see some benefit from that. I could actually see where the jobs are going to come from. But I cannot. I do not understand how it will work. I do not understand where we are going to create work for the people involved.
We will pass the bill at six o'clock, as far as we are concerned, and the government can go ahead with the business of getting the money out, if there is someone to take advantage of it. My suspicion about this is that what is going to happen is that some of the money will be used to pay for employees in jobs that already exist, not new jobs, and that in fact a lot of this money will not be taken advantage of because there will be no new jobs. In the final analysis there will be an everincreasing number of people unemployed, and we still will not have in place a major strategy for dealing with the chaos that confronts most of the economic sectors in the country. I really do believe that we are dealing with this in a very backward way.
The minister could have the bill passed and could get on with it if he could bring in some kind of economic strategy to show where we are going to create employment in the long term. I have not seen, heard or have any inkling as to when that is going to come or, for that matter, whether it is ever going to come. I suspect it is not. I do not think the government has the foggiest idea how to deal with it.

Mr. Chairman, I am happy to speak on the extension of the employment tax credit program. I know that program well, having worked in a Canada Manpower Centre as an adviser, and I am in a position to tell you that it is a little gem, and it is so for several reasons.
First of all, when that project was created, the government tried to set up a program that could apply without adding to the pile of paper work an employer normally has to cope with when he operates under a government program.
It has always been said that, whether here or elsewhere at any level of government, there is always too much red tape, too many meetings with officials, too many all sorts of things. If some of my hon. colleagues ever worked with the tax credit program, the only paper the Canada Manpower Centre fills in is a yellow form that certifies the hiring of an employee, and the employer at the end of the year only has to send a form to Revenue Canada on which he puts the salary, and that is all. That is it and it is an incentive that people had a little difficulty with at first because there are two departments involved, the Department of National Revenue and the Department of Employment and Immigration. At first there was a little lack of confidence between the officials of each department. In the third year of application, it was a phenomenal success. If the program is being extended today for another year, it is quite simply because it is a necessity.
I come from an area where the rate of unemployment varies regularly between 15 per cent and 20 per cent. We have a huge problem to live with, and that problem is all the more serious as it affects particularly young people. In an area like mine with multinational industries, most of those industries are unionized, the unions are very strong, and like any good union, they protect the seniority of their workers, and that is normal. But the result of all that is that those who have to suffer from the problem of unemployment are the young people.
I heard a while ago some colleagues criticize the existing job-creation program which this government launched in the early seventies, and all I can say is that I wonder, had we not spent that money to create so many jobs every year, year after year, how our young people could have kept their self-respect. Of course, the job-creation activity is not creating permanent jobs, but jobs to allow young people to subsist while the real work problems are being resolved. By the way, we have had such a large number of people coming out on the labour market, a number larger than any other country has seen, when women started to go out to work and when young people from the generation born during the years 1945 to 1960 started to appear on the labour market 15 years ago. There were too
June 11, 1980

many of those young people at the same time and the work they did was not really necessary. They were supported by temporary program like Canada Works, LIP or that kind of program assisted by an Unemployment Insurance Act which allowed them to live decently, with a sense of self-respect.
The ETCP is another program which aims at getting at the roots of the problem. This program can really promote job creation. An employer in my constituency is happy to receive a tax credit of $1.75 an hour when he hires a young worker, and generally, this young worker will stay with this business afterwards.
Farm workers can also benefit from the program. They are very happy about it. It is the nicest little program ever conceived because it can be applied easily. There is no need to hire ten accountants to be told what to do and what form must be filled in and sent back to the government. I therefore find it difficult to understand why the discussion has gone on for so long to extend this program for one year. It is easy to draw conclusions, but the gentlemen opposite, as our friends in Quebec often say, the hon. members on the other side should go and see in their own constituencies the people who have used this program. It is a real jewel. When you talk to them about a manpower training program, they will tell you: that is very nice, but we have to consult the province for a training program. However, you set up something when you were in power not so long ago and you knew that it would come to an end on March 31-

I believe that there is a great potential of use in this program, and the minister will confirm that the funds allocated to the ETCP in the last two years were not sufficient because there always were more requests. This proves that this program is effective and will be increasingly so to the extent, first of all, that members of Parliament will publicize it in their ridings at the same time as the department and will tell their constituents about it because it is universal and applies to nearly everyone. This is one of the elements that the government conceived to fight the basic problem of unemployment which affects all the countries of the capitalistic or western world.
Over the past ten years Canada has given people billions and told them: "Think of ideas, we will give you money, do what you like". There is no other country in the world which did that and it proves that we are confident in the possibilities of the population, and that is why Mr. Pierre Trudeau was re-elected as Prime Minister of Canada during the last federal election. Besides proving that we have faith in the people this
Employment Tax Credit Act
constituted an opinion poll which we do not often have the chance to see because it is not one in which we ask people: "Are you for or against this issue?" It is an opinion poll which asks the individual what he thinks. We give money to someone who uses it however he sees fit. The results are fantastic. In my area, job-creation projects have worked wonders which can be used today for recreation purposes or others. Apart from this, there is also the fact that permanent institutions were created from temporary projects. And all this in the context of the same employment tax credit program. A little while ago, I heard someone ask who is going to create jobs. There is no one here on this side of the House who can claim to know the truth and to be able to create all the necessary jobs in Canada. No one. What we are saying is that within this country there are a good many people who have an incredible potential to create jobs and for the last 12 years we have been helping them. That is why Canada has one of the lowest unemployment rates in the world as well as one of the lowest inflation rates. We will continue to do what we have done, to have faith in the population, in all Canadians. This is what is being done in my area and I am happy to encourage these people.
A little while ago, we were talking about a striking committee for job creation. That is essential. When we came to power and the previous government had decided, oh wonder, to put an end to the job-creation program, to suppress it, we wound up with the program pretty much in tatters; the striking committees had disappeared. We had to take all that in hand and rebuild. People ask me: Why a striking committee? Because these striking committees are comprised of key people who have ideas, know the local background, come from all parts of the region and from every corner of the riding; these people sit down and study ideas which are presented to them and invest money in them. It is simply a question of trusting the people. If you trust Canadians, Canadians will trust you. We know what we are talking about. We have been in power almost 20 years. That is essential. When you want to show someone you trust him you give him the opportunity of making it on his own. That is exactly what we are doing. We are not the fountain of truth. We will not force Canadians to work in areas they do not want to work or to do things they do not want to do, but we will help them hire other Canadians, if they want, and put their ideas in practice.
In conclusion I wonder if the minister could tell us whether the budget for the tax credit program, with which I became very familiar when I worked at the Canada Manpower Centre, will be increased over last year? I am aware of the fact that the program is being extended another year. Perhaps it should be extended even longer, but I wonder whether the program budget itself, and I realize these are hard times, can be increased.

Mr. Chairman, I want to make a few comments and ask the minister a couple of questions. Nobody has a monopoly on the concern, which we all must share in the crisis that we have, over unemployment and other related problems of the economy. I agree with the minister that there is not one simple solution to this serious problem. However, we on this side differ from this government in the approach. The former government attempted to create jobs of a more permanent nature. This government has gone back to the grand mentality which emerged in the early 1970s where it makes money available to keep people working for three or four months so that they can qualify for unemployment insurance. I realize, though, that there must be such a program, especially when the economy has been mismanaged as badly as it has, not only by Canada-but by other countries as well.
Has the minister or his department been involved in discussions with the provincial governments with regard to this whole area of manpower training? It is quite obvious to me, as it is to many Canadians today, that there is something fundamentally wrong with our primary and secondary education processes. We are keeping our young people in school far too long, and this has a twofold effect. When we keep young people in school for 13 years-I am talking particularly about young people who are motivated at the ages of 15, 16 or 17 toward some kind of a job skill-to prepare them for a career,
they are bored to death. This system provides nothing more than a babysitting service.
As a result, we are graduating from our schools today armies of young people with no job skills and who have lost all their motivation toward a certain trade skill. Because the education process has been disrupted, we have academic mediocrity as well. Is it not high time that the various governments get together and work out a program?
Indeed, the educational program in the province of Ontario provides for such a scheme in which young people are offered a training position in industry. They are offered the opportunity to leave school at grade nine or ten, find a place in industry- not at $9 per hour, but at $1.50 per hour because they are continuing to learn a trade and a skill. This learning experience within the industry would be supplemented with training, perhaps one day a week or one week a month, in one of the colleges or secondary schools in the country.
The minister will readily recognize that what I have described is the European system. There is a model of that system functioning in Ottawa right now, and the academic portion of it will run into September. The question is, have there been any discussions with the provinces to address this very fundamental problem, which will help to prepare us for the 1980s and, indeed, for the next century when we will need highly skilled people to work at highly technical jobs?
I would also like to know if there have been any discussions with the unions and the industries and whether these two groups are concerned about this problem. We cannot expect the federal government to find a solution to what is probably the most crucial problem facing our country today, particularly as it refers to youth unemployment. It is a problem which no single agency can solve by itself. It is a problem which requires the input of the federal government, the provincial governments, the industries and, of course, the workers' organizations, before an agreement can be reached.
Can the minister enlighten us as to whether he is concerned as well about these matters, whether there are any discussions going on and whether he has read some of the studies which have been produced by some of my colleagues, by educators in the country, and so on? What does the minister see for the future with regard to the combination of manpower training and job creation, which are two areas for which his department is responsible?
